staticMetadata.guideSummary: Caparica beachbreak near the main Costa da Caparica report cluster.

This sandy alcove, sandwiched between two, long, rocky groynes, looks across to Lisbon from the southern fringe of the Tejo / Tagus rivermouth. When a big swell hits, the accumulated sand throws up powerful, short, wedgy waves popular with a loyal bodyboarding crew. There is a right breaking off the northern groyne, as well as a left to the south. The waves are hollow and heavy. The swell angle is important as the rivermouth can cut out some of the size.

travelDetails.description: Just 15 minutes outside Lisbon, this wave features heavy, sand-bottom barrels, especially in wintertime when it's really cranking. And though the waves may look unmakeable when you take off, if you hold a high line and hang tight, you're looking at an 85 percent success rate. The waves in summer are fairly inconsistent, as it's tucked pretty far in to get the short-period windswell that lights up the beachbreaks around Ericeira and Peniche. But come autumn, and straight through into spring, the waves march in around the corner, peaking up and down the hard-packed sandbars.
travelDetails.hazards: Crowds and hitting bottom on bigger days.

staticMetadata.guideSummary:
The Reef is a little finger of lava that sticks out at the far south tip of the Ribeira Bay. North swells come in from deep water, peak up on an outside rock and fold over themselves down the line in one of the fastest, and most dangerous, tubes around.

There are no cutback sections, really, and very little room for error. If you blow the drop, you're up on sharp, dry reef. But if you're able to snag one off the locals and make the ledgey drop from behind the peak, you're in for a fantastic four-second view. Just remember to avoid going for that floater on the inside section.

There are a few other waves close by, if you're not in the mood for tight tubes and reef dances: Piedra Branca (White Rock) is a hollow, high-tide left about 100 yards south. There's a slightly mushy right just south of the Reef, and on bigger swells, a left breaks off the north edge.

*ERICEIRA WORLD SURFING RESERVE*

travelDetails.description:
The cliff lined sandy bay, the reeling right hand walls that speed down the line, back off, then speed through to the finish on the inside. Part of its quality comes in its flexibility - it starts breaking at just over knee high and keeps going to double overhead or more - pumping out huge, winding faces that can run for over 200m. There is also a reef on the outside northern edge of the main break called Pontinha, a right hander that works best in medium swells. *ERICEIRA WORLD SURFING RESERVE*

staticMetadata.guideSummary:
Europe's best right, Coxos is the crown jewel of Portugal. The wave, which is like a reef/pointbreak, breaks along a shallow rock shelf into a very small bay. Swells muscle their way in from deep water just offshore and form into fast-moving symmetrical right walls that seem to concentrate all their power into the base of the wave rather than the lip, similar to many Hawaiian waves. There's no easy entry at Coxos. You've got to paddle like mad, get to your feet and start driving, otherwise you'll get sucked over and end up on the reef.

*ERICEIRA WORLD SURFING RESERVE*

shoulderBurn.description: Definitely some work on the bigger and better days.

spotRating.description: One of the best waves in the country when it is working.

staticMetadata.guideSummary: Consolação is the fortress-adorned headland at the southern end of Supertubos beach. It delivers nice, heavy waves on both sides: a reefy, although somewhat fat, right-hand pointbreak, and a heavy, more stacked up sand-bottomed left. The right is a local favorite when the swell wraps around the headland and can hold size up to triple overhead. The left needs bigger swells to come to life and is a more volatile and dependable on sand placement on the bottom.

abilityLevels.description: Intermediate to advanced. Above 10 ft. both waves require fully developed skills.

tide.description: Mid tide brings out the point’s best shape.

crowdFactor.description: Busy, focused. Consolação is capable of holding form when Supertubos is maxing out, so there are lots of surfers flocking to it for more manageable waves. Rarely over 20 people at the same time on the right, even less on the left.

localVibe.description: Don’t expect smiles or greetings when approaching the line-up, but stink-eyes and hassles are not a common thing neither. Approach carefully, let a couple of sets pass you by before catching one, and you should be fine.

shoulderBurn.description: Long paddles for both sides of the spot, harder on the left because of the shorebreak and multiple foam lines.

spotRating.description: Pointbreak over reef with reliable walls on the right. Longer, faster and steeper walls on the left.

waterQuality.description: Clean. A regular recipient of the Quercus Golden Quality award, Consolação is widely known and sought-after for its iodine concentrations and therapeutic properties.

travelDetails.access: Beachfront parking by the fortress.

travelDetails.description: The central stretch of Peniche’s North Bay features a sandy bottom and offers different banks with multiple left and right peaks suitable for all skill levels. An ideal spot for both beginners and intermediate surfers, it can form pretty mellow rides with the occasional barrel. The wavelength can vary depending on swell size, period, and the shape of the sand banks. A good getaway spot for south wind days when most of Portugal’s coast is onshore.

staticMetadata.guideSummary: A lesser-known beachbreak at the south end of Peniche’s north bay (Baía), right at the city’s entry. Cerro offers softer beachbreak waves and quieter sessions. Ideal for a mellow surf or when looking to avoid the crowds at Supertubos or Baleal. Consistent throughout the year, even on average days there’s potential for some long rides if the banks align.

abilityLevels.description: Beginner to intermediate.

tide.description: Mid tide is the go-to, but low tide can fire if the sandbars are good.

windDirection.description: E–NE is ideal but rideable with light onshores and west swell.

swellDirection.description: Works best on NW swell with E–NE wind.

bottom.description: Sand with rocky patches where a lobster farm used to operate back in the day.

crowdFactor.description: Quiet, mellow, friendly but it can get pretty crowded, especially with surf schools and tourists.

localVibe.description: Cerro is mostly surfed by tourists and beginners. The atmosphere is welcoming and family-friendly but beware of loose boards and inexperienced surfers.

shoulderBurn.description: Easy.

spotRating.description: Low-key beachbreak with variable sandbars, capable of providing fun rides but hardly thrilling ones.

waterQuality.description: Clean. Recipient of the Quercus Golden Quality certification.

travelDetails.access: Roadside parking, beach access.

travelDetails.hazards: Occasional rip currents, inexperienced apprentices, and the occasional submerge rocks.

staticMetadata.guideSummary: Corner of the bay that likes northerly to northwesterly swell and clean east-side winds.

abilityLevels.description: Good for all abilities, especially when small, can get hollow and reeling when bigger.

season.description: Consistent spot, best September to November and March to May.

tide.description: All tides - there is a small section of high tide rocks north of cafe.

bottom.description: Sand with small section of hight tide rocks.

crowdFactor.description: Popular spot, in certain swells can be one of the few places working so gets busy.

localVibe.description: OK, popular with travelling and local surfers, plus surf schools.

shoulderBurn.description: OK but occasionally heavy when size picks up.

spotRating.description: Fun, flexible beach break with good quality walling waves - predominantly rights. Can get hollow. Popular with beginners when small.

waterQuality.description: OK

travelDetails.access: Parking either by the beachside cafe or in the large car park to the north.
travelDetails.description: Cantinho Da Baia - 'corner of the bay' is an area that comes to life in a big northerly, or medium sized northwesterly swell and offers clean waves and winds from northeast to southeast direction. Long, sometimes hollow rights can peel here. Consistent and fun, popular with beginners when small.

staticMetadata.guideSummary: Peniche/Baleal surf hub with Lagide and open beachbreak nearby.

abilityLevels.description: Depends on the size but you can typically find a smaller and more protected wave for the newer surfers on either side of the peninsula depending on swell and wind.

season.description: Autumn and Spring -- wind and weather can be issues in the Winter.

tide.description: Mid to lower tide typically best.

windDirection.description: Northeast for Baleal and southeast or even south for Lagide and Ferrel.

bottom.description: Sand, except for the reef at Lagide.

crowdFactor.description: As long as you avoid the surf schools and Lagide, crowds shouldn't be too much of a problem.

localVibe.description: There's no shortage of barking at Lagide. It's generally not worth the hassle anyways, but if you do paddle out, be respectful and don't drop in on any bodyboarders.

shoulderBurn.description: Depends on the size and which zone you surf.

spotRating.description: Pretty average.

waterQuality.description: Not bad.

travelDetails.access: There's a big parking lot right at Lagide where campers congregate. The beachbreaks north are accessed via a dirt track that runs along the coast.
travelDetails.description: Baleal has been a big destination for traveling surfers for more than 20 years. Most of the learn-to-surf camps in Portugal are located here. With the mellow left reefbreak of Lagide just north of town, followed by miles of open beachbreak, you can have a pretty high surfer population density without too many problems.

staticMetadata.guideSummary: Northern Baleal reef/point area with lefts over shallow rocks.

abilityLevels.description: A great wave for all levels, but the degree of crowd means it's best left to experienced surfers only.

season.description: Consistent spot, best September to November and March to May.

tide.description: Best low to mid tide.

crowdFactor.description: Can get very busy.

localVibe.description: Competitive.

shoulderBurn.description: Easy paddle out.

spotRating.description: Super fun, long walling reef with smashable sections that stays fun even as size picks up.

waterQuality.description: OK

travelDetails.access: Car park overlooks reef.
travelDetails.description: This long, super-fun left sits in front of the car-park at Lagide and is the first thing you see when you pull up. There's a mellow take off, before it walls up into a reeling top to bottom lefthander that peels and peels over a flat reef. There's a dry hair paddle out around the break. All this adds up to one thing - crowds. The take-off point is tiny and many try to take off deep /on the wrong side of the peak to steal a march on the masses.

staticMetadata.guideSummary: A wall of crumbly, red sandstone cliffs looks out over this huge expanse of golden sand that stretches from Baleal northeast to the Obidos Lagoon. One of the highlights is Almagreira, home to some consistent banks that work through the tides. Picks up loads of swell so super consistent, but easily blown out.

abilityLevels.description: Good for all abilities, remote so take care.

season.description: A real swell catcher that works all year but best September to November.

tide.description: All tides - beach can disappear at high.

crowdFactor.description: If busy, walk up beach as there are many peaks to chose from.

localVibe.description: OK, but this stretch used to be mostly locals and is now getting busy, so humility and respect will serve you well.

shoulderBurn.description: Ok but can get heavy when size picks up.

spotRating.description: Long stretch of consistent beach break that can produce some fun, occasionally hollow banks.

waterQuality.description: OK

travelDetails.access: Accessed via rough piste roads, parking on cliff top, don't leave valuables in the car. Cliff access prone to erosion.

staticMetadata.guideSummary:
While surfed sporadically earlier, the world's biggest, baddest, most oversized wedge, Nazaré took center stage in the big wave world after Garrett MacNamara was invited there to "surf the world's biggest wave" in 2011. Since then, Nazaré has become a household name, one of Portugal's main coastal tourist attractions, a (former) stop on the Big Wave World Tour, and ground zero for big wave tow surfing. On the days when the offshore canyon isn't focusing huge swells into 80-foot peaks, Nazaré's inside sand bar produces heavy, hollow tubes in sizes that mortals can appreciate (as long as those mortals are barrel-riding experts).

LINEUP TIPS: Etiquette | Surf Safety Basics

abilityLevels.description: Inside beach break is for experienced barrel hounds and pros. XXL Nazaré is for the world's best big wave surfers only.

season.description: Swell season extends from October through March, although it tends to get colder and stormier the further into winter you go.

tide.description: Works on all tides, but is best on a mid incoming tide.

windDirection.description: Light to moderate wind from the E to SE is best.

swellDirection.description: W through NW works, with WNW swells receiving the most constructive interference from the offshore canyon.

bottom.description: Sand bar, ranging from shallow near the shore break to quite deep on big days.

crowdFactor.description: Small local crowd on inside days, tow circus on big days.

localVibe.description: Nazaré has become one of Portugal's favorite spectacles, and the local population tends to love surfing (and especially the surfers who brave Nazaré). That being said, the lineup can get a bit hectic on the biggest days.

shoulderBurn.description: Possibly the most difficult big wave spot in the world to paddle due to a complete lack of channel or safe zone.

spotRating.description: The world's biggest wave, and an A+ beach break barrel on small days.

waterQuality.description: Although the wave breaks a short distance from a moderate sized coastal town, the water remains pretty clean.

travelDetails.access: Drive from Lisbon to the town of Nazaré, arrange a jet ski, and access the wave via the harbor. On smaller days, paddle out at Praia do Norte.
